overall: The AG found the Board did not violate the Open Meeting Law in the ways alleged: it declined two complaints (Rule of Necessity; minutes already decided in OML 2020-156) and found no violation on the rest.

allegations.summary: Complaints alleged the Board discussed topics not on the August 24 and September 28 notices: media/Facebook allegations about a member's conduct, and a dilapidated garage.
allegations.key_passage: We find that these discussions naturally flowed from the Board’s consideration of the posted agenda topic and therefore the Board did not violate the Open Meeting Law.

allegations.summary: Complaint alleged the Board failed to approve minutes of eight meetings (May 28 to July 30) in a timely manner.
allegations.key_passage: We decline to review this allegation because we have already decided the issue in a previous determination.

allegations.summary: Complaint alleged the Board improperly used the Rule of Necessity to allow a conflicted member to participate.
allegations.key_passage: Even if true, the allegation in this complaint regarding a violation of the Rule of Necessity, which allows a public body member to participate in a meeting even though he is disqualified due to a conflict of interest because, without the member’s participation, the public body would not otherwise have a quorum, would not constitute a violation of the Open Meeting Law.

allegations.summary: Complaints alleged the Board did not give the former Health Agent 48 hours' written notice before the September 10 executive session on her employment.
allegations.key_passage: We need not resolve this discrepancy here because we find that the Board also sent an email to Ms. Freire-Kellogg’s attorney on September 8 advising him of the intended executive session discussions regarding his client for the Board’s September 10 meeting.

allegations.summary: Complaint alleged the chair did not let the former Health Agent speak on her own behalf during the August 24 meeting discussion about her.
allegations.key_passage: Therefore, because it is within the chair’s discretion to limit public participation during a meeting, the chair did not violate the Open Meeting Law by preventing Ms. Freire-Kellogg from addressing the Board in open session.
